rationale: The moments benchmark is a Shootout-C++ numeric program: a handful of small functions dominated by tight floating-point loops over input data, so nearly all execution time concentrates in a very hot inner loop while static code size and function count are tiny. To maximize reverse-engineering resistance without wrecking the hot loop, I weight heavily toward low-cost, high-diversity passes: SUB (arithmetic substitution) and SPLIT (which also improves the effectiveness of downstream passes) get strong Security/Diversity weights with generous cost tolerance, and IGV and ICALL are kept moderately enabled since indirect globals and calls add static-analysis friction at modest runtime price. Conversely, BCF, FLA, and IBR are the expensive control-flow passes — bogus branches and flattening multiply basic blocks inside precisely the loops this benchmark re-executes millions of times, and IBR's indirect branches pressure the branch predictor — so their RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights are deliberately kept low (0.2-0.3) to throttle their selection. CorrectnessRisk weights stay low across the board (0.1-0.3) because the program is straight-line scalar/FP computation with no volatile access, inline asm, setjmp, or unusual ABI surface, so even aggressive transformation is unlikely to break semantics; the slightly elevated risk on BCF/FLA/IBR simply reflects extra control-flow rewriting on FP-heavy code.
